newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thailand bites the bullet, or is it just a nibble?.
newsitem.headline: Thailand bites the bullet, or is it just a nibble?.

text.p: Thailand sparked turmoil in Asian financial markets on Wednesday by announcing it would adopt a "managed float" policy on the baht, a move which was initially interpreted as a one-off big-bang devaluation.
But there is a big question mark over how far and how fast the Thai authorities will allow the baht to fall, despite the fact that the currency plunged on the news.

"The problem in the past was with the exchange arrangements rather than with the level of the exchange rate," said Kobus van der Wath, Regional Head of Treasury Economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
"In that sense I don't think the new reference point will be too far away from previous levels. Despite the balloon going up today I still think they will go for the slowly does it approach."
The Bank of Thailand said it would set a daily dollar/baht reference point and had an "appropriate rate" in mind in which it expected the baht to move.
This is somewhat similar to the old system whereby the baht was fixed against a basket of currencies and kept within a four satang range around that, but on the face of it allows more flexibility.
Although Thai interest rates had to be immediately raised two points to 12.5 percent prevent a currency meltdown, a more flexible exchange rate policy will allow rates to ultimately come down.

"In the short-term there will be uncertainty and volatility but beyond that what they have done gives more flexibility to policy makers in adjusting interest rates down," said Ng Bok Eng, Regional Economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore.
"And given the current backdrop, the economy is in desperate need of easier credit policy," he added.

So it seems the Thai authorities are willing to let the economy take it on the chin in the near-term as regards higher rates and manage the currency down gradually while regaining investor confidence.
This could be similar to the Indonesian system where Bank Indonesia has adopted a crawling exchange rate peg whereby the rupiah is allowed to gradually edge down on the U.S. dollar.
The return of confidence is key as it is this which will would allow interest rates to come down in the medium-term.

The baht was first attacked in mid May when it was trading around 26.000 to the U.S. dollar. After the dust settled on Wednesday it was quoted at around 28.00 in the offshore market and around 27.000 in the onshore market. But volume was light.
"There is no trading going on, these rates are pretty much on an indicative basis only," said one dealer.

Since the speculative attack on the currency in May the Thai authorities have battled to maintain the value of the baht by intervening aggressively and in a more draconian move by re-introducing capital controls.
The two-tier market grew up after exchange controls were imposed, effectively cutting off the supply of baht to offshore speculators from local sources.

But this inflexibility brought it own problems and the situation became unsustainable as investor confidence haemorrhaged. Thailand's currency account gap means it relies on inward capital flows and confidence and investment are two sides of the same coin.
"Clearly their backs were to the wall given the speculative attack on the baht and I think these measures are aimed at boosting confidence," Standard's van der Wath said.
"But fixing a reference point for the baht allows them to set the pace."
